title: One intended operation
intro: A caller asks for one release ticket. The intended effect is one saved ticket, not merely a successful network response.
takeaway: Separate the business effect from the response that reports it.

beats.text: The caller wants one release ticket. The service must save that effect.
The create request reaches the service. The service begins the operation.
The service saves ticket 47. The database records that effect.
A response reports ticket 47. This normal attempt succeeds.

title: A missing reply
intro: The service saves a ticket but the reply is lost. The caller times out without knowing whether the operation happened.
takeaway: A timeout does not prove that nothing was created. Retrying an unprotected create can duplicate the effect.

beats.text: The caller sends a create request. The service receives it.
The service saves ticket 47. Its response will not reach the caller.
The caller stops waiting. Its outcome is unknown.
Another create could add a duplicate. The caller needs a stable operation ID.

title: Name the operation
intro: The caller saves key k7 with its release request before sending. The service commits the ticket and key record in one database transaction.
takeaway: The key identifies an intended operation. Atomic storage and uniqueness are needed to prevent concurrent duplicate effects in this design.

beats.text: New attempt: save key k7 before sending. This time, protect the operation upfront.
Send the key with the request. The service checks its stored records.
The first attempt creates ticket 47. Store the ticket and key atomically.
Suppose this protected reply is lost too. Key k7 still identifies the saved ticket.

title: Retry the same key
intro: After losing the response, the caller resends k7 with the same release payload. The service finds the previous result.
takeaway: The retry reuses the recorded effect instead of creating a second ticket. This depends on the service contract and key retention.

beats.text: The caller still needs its result. It reuses the saved key k7.
The service looks up k7. Its record points to ticket 47.
The existing result is returned. No second ticket is created.
The caller receives ticket 47. The intended effect remains one ticket.

title: Changed intent, new key
intro: The caller now sends a different release payload using the old key. This service compares the stored payload before deciding whether replay is valid.
takeaway: A key is not a general-purpose deduplication label. Reusing it for changed intent must follow the service contract; here the request is rejected.

beats.text: Key k7 belongs to release v1. The new payload asks for release v2.
The service compares the payloads. The same key now has different intent.
The service rejects the mismatch. It does not overwrite the old operation.
A new operation needs a new key. A retry keeps its original identity.
